beats.new_visual_element: What chapter 2 covers, and what I reviewed
beats.narration: Chapter 2 covers five major sections: defining cancer and uncontrolled growth, the history of cancer research, the hallmarks of cancer, oncology terminology, and cancer epidemiology. It is one of the largest chapters in the textbook, and it took a careful, systematic review to work through.

beats.narration: I reviewed 46 claims in the main tab, 134 sentences in the AI-only tab, and 8 editorial issues. Of the 46 main claims, 25 were confirmed true, 18 were false, and 3 were flagged for ambiguity. That is a much higher error rate than Chapter 1, where most claims checked out.

beats.new_visual_element: What the textbook says, and what the current number is
beats.narration: The biggest pattern I found was stale data. Six claims in the History of Cancer Research section all came from the same 2021 commemorative article and have not been updated for a 2026 textbook. For example, the text says there are 71 NCI-Designated Cancer Centers, but the current count is 74. It says about 100 targeted therapies have been approved, but the real number is now over 157.

beats.new_visual_element: Where did this number come from?
beats.narration: I found the same problem in the Epidemiology section. Three claims were pulled word for word from a 2007 WHO publication, making them nearly 20 years out of date. The numbers on obesity, occupational exposure, and hepatitis B have all changed significantly since then.

beats.new_visual_element: 134 sentences the AI said needed no review, 3 errors found
beats.narration: Even in the AI-only tab, where the AI flagged sentences as not needing human review, I caught three errors. One reversed a well-known biological pathway. Another placed a 12th-century scholar in the 13th century. And a third garbled one of Hanahan and Weinberg's six hallmarks of cancer. These are exactly the kinds of mistakes that slip through without human review.

beats.narration: Chapter 2 reinforced something I keep seeing in this work: AI-generated text tends to grab numbers from whatever source it trained on, without checking whether those numbers are still current. For a medical textbook, that is not good enough. Every claim needs verification.

artifactLines: A number can be real and still be out of date.

Check the date on the source, not just the source.
Every claim needs verification. Chapter 2 was 39% false.

beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the viewer's prompt typed
beats.narration: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take a document that quotes statistics and pick five of them. For each one, find the original source and check the date on it, not just whether the source exists. Tell me which numbers are current, which were true once and have since moved, and which you cannot date at all. Do not tell me whether the number sounds plausible. A stale number always sounds plausible. That is the whole problem.
